Technology has always been a disruptor, but AI is arguably moving faster than the technology reforms that have come before it, and the best ways to be using it are also less understood than with previous innovations, making skills development even harder.

UK government has implemented many schemes and initiatives aiming to increase digital, and especially AI, skills across all levels, including an £11.7m Digital Inclusion Innovation Fund invested in 80 digital skills programmes, and a £200m fund aimed at upskilling businesses and helping them adopt and scale AI, among other things.

But Brewin questioned whether the government fully understands the scale of impact AI will have on both education and work, and said there needs to be a combined “socio-technical” approach to adopting the technology that considers both the capabilities of it and how it can be used, as well as the social implications of doing so.

He expressed concern about the government’s current approach to AI adoption, stating it is heavy on promoting technical capabilities without thinking about the “social dimensions” of doing so, and pointed out that this is especially poignant in schools where AI is being trialled for a number of functions.

“[An] extremely powerful set of technologies could be dropped in [to schools] without really thinking about the social implications on the fundamentally important ecosystem of relationships that is so precious in schools within learning,” said Brewin.

No more junior roles?

Another concern across the tech sector is the possibility that AI will eliminate entry-level jobs as the technology is increasingly implemented to take care of the administrative tasks usually allotted to junior staffers.

Hillman claimed entry-level jobs are “exposed” by rapid AI adoption and the changes that brings, not only because AI can be used to automate entry level tasks, but also because firms are usually unwilling to make hiring decisions when the climate is uncertain which “hits entry-level roles first”, flagging it as an area that needs “attention” from the government.

On the flipside, he claimed: “Graduates probably on average are having more experience of using AI as part of their education, so they are acquiring some of the AI literacy, which means when they’re entering those roles, they are probably better able to immediately apply some of those in the workplace in a sophisticated way.”

This again puts pressure on young people to be learning how to appropriately use AI and apply it to their lives and the workplace without necessarily having been taught how to do so in schools, with Brewin stating: “The basket of skills that young people are being asked to bring to a first job has grown.

“The demand is bigger for them, which puts a huge onus on young people there.”

Parents are even beginning to change the career advice they give their children as a result of AI adoption, and young people believe it will make getting a job more difficult when their time comes, with Will Akrigg, UK government affairs manager at The King’s Trust, claiming AI is “changing the picture” of employment of young people across the UK.

An increasing number of people in the UK are not in education, employment or training (Neet), and while AI is not solely to blame, Akrigg said it’s having a “massive impact on the job market generally”.

Not only are employers expecting more and more skills, but AI is heavily used in the recruitment process, and it’s “disheartening” for young people looking for jobs.

The divide

Another disheartening concern for young people in the wake of AI is its potential to widen the diversity gap in the tech sector. Where it is already more difficult for young people from lower-income backgrounds to enter a tech role, AI could serve to make it even harder.

Hillman said: “We’re probably overestimating the changes that are happening in the short term and are underestimating the long-term change, but the direction of travel is quite clear – AI is changing work across a wide swathe of occupations and sectors unevenly.

“[AI is] definitely narrowing the number of opportunities for those young people, and it’s also changing the nature of those jobs, but I think it’s particularly going to be challenging for those young people who have lower-level qualifications, or struggled to get work experience and work readiness through their pathways.”

Access to digital across the UK is already uneven, both as a result of different socio-economic circumstances, disability and geographic discrepancies, and while AI has the potential to help this, it also has the potential to exacerbate it if implemented incorrectly.

As pointed out by Milnes: “If you can’t even get reliable internet, you’re obviously not going to be able to use AI in the same transformative manner.”

The UK government has been working to use AI to develop free-to-use tutoring tools in schools across the UK with the view of making educational resources more easily accessible to students regardless of their socio-economic background, helping to level the playing field for those who, in many cases, do not have access to technology at home or are unable to afford private tutoring.

But there is no “quick fix”, warned Neil Selwyn, professor at Monash University. “I’m worried there is a tendency to see AI as a quick fix for students who are struggling in school,” he said.

“There’s no quick fix for learners who are from social deprived multiply disadvantaged backgrounds; I think we do need to invest in people and resources and time,” said Selwyn. “Tech can be part of that in the background, but I don’t think technology is ever going to be the solution to any kind of social disadvantage issue.”

It’s clear that AI is changing work, education and mindsets, but only careful consideration will ensure young people will have equal access to the careers they want.

As Luckin surmised: “Most of my time as an academic I believed AI would be a great tool for breaking down barriers, for greater inclusion, and it’s not rolling out that way at the moment, and we really need to be careful about that.”

  • With the appropriate training, artificial intelligence could stand to be a productivity booster and job search equaliser, according to Okta’s chief marketing officer, Shannon Duffy.

Technology has always been a disruptor, but AI is arguably moving faster than the technology reforms that have come before it, and the best ways to be using it are also less understood than with previous innovations, making skills development even harder.

UK government has implemented many schemes and initiatives aiming to increase digital, and especially AI, skills across all levels, including an £11.7m Digital Inclusion Innovation Fund invested in 80 digital skills programmes, and a £200m fund aimed at upskilling businesses and helping them adopt and scale AI, among other things.

But Brewin questioned whether the government fully understands the scale of impact AI will have on both education and work, and said there needs to be a combined “socio-technical” approach to adopting the technology that considers both the capabilities of it and how it can be used, as well as the social implications of doing so.

He expressed concern about the government’s current approach to AI adoption, stating it is heavy on promoting technical capabilities without thinking about the “social dimensions” of doing so, and pointed out that this is especially poignant in schools where AI is being trialled for a number of functions.

“[An] extremely powerful set of technologies could be dropped in [to schools] without really thinking about the social implications on the fundamentally important ecosystem of relationships that is so precious in schools within learning,” said Brewin.

No more junior roles?

Another concern across the tech sector is the possibility that AI will eliminate entry-level jobs as the technology is increasingly implemented to take care of the administrative tasks usually allotted to junior staffers.

Hillman claimed entry-level jobs are “exposed” by rapid AI adoption and the changes that brings, not only because AI can be used to automate entry level tasks, but also because firms are usually unwilling to make hiring decisions when the climate is uncertain which “hits entry-level roles first”, flagging it as an area that needs “attention” from the government.

On the flipside, he claimed: “Graduates probably on average are having more experience of using AI as part of their education, so they are acquiring some of the AI literacy, which means when they’re entering those roles, they are probably better able to immediately apply some of those in the workplace in a sophisticated way.”

This again puts pressure on young people to be learning how to appropriately use AI and apply it to their lives and the workplace without necessarily having been taught how to do so in schools, with Brewin stating: “The basket of skills that young people are being asked to bring to a first job has grown.

“The demand is bigger for them, which puts a huge onus on young people there.”

Parents are even beginning to change the career advice they give their children as a result of AI adoption, and young people believe it will make getting a job more difficult when their time comes, with Will Akrigg, UK government affairs manager at The King’s Trust, claiming AI is “changing the picture” of employment of young people across the UK.

An increasing number of people in the UK are not in education, employment or training (Neet), and while AI is not solely to blame, Akrigg said it’s having a “massive impact on the job market generally”.

Not only are employers expecting more and more skills, but AI is heavily used in the recruitment process, and it’s “disheartening” for young people looking for jobs.

The divide

Another disheartening concern for young people in the wake of AI is its potential to widen the diversity gap in the tech sector. Where it is already more difficult for young people from lower-income backgrounds to enter a tech role, AI could serve to make it even harder.

Hillman said: “We’re probably overestimating the changes that are happening in the short term and are underestimating the long-term change, but the direction of travel is quite clear – AI is changing work across a wide swathe of occupations and sectors unevenly.

“[AI is] definitely narrowing the number of opportunities for those young people, and it’s also changing the nature of those jobs, but I think it’s particularly going to be challenging for those young people who have lower-level qualifications, or struggled to get work experience and work readiness through their pathways.”

Access to digital across the UK is already uneven, both as a result of different socio-economic circumstances, disability and geographic discrepancies, and while AI has the potential to help this, it also has the potential to exacerbate it if implemented incorrectly.

As pointed out by Milnes: “If you can’t even get reliable internet, you’re obviously not going to be able to use AI in the same transformative manner.”

The UK government has been working to use AI to develop free-to-use tutoring tools in schools across the UK with the view of making educational resources more easily accessible to students regardless of their socio-economic background, helping to level the playing field for those who, in many cases, do not have access to technology at home or are unable to afford private tutoring.

But there is no “quick fix”, warned Neil Selwyn, professor at Monash University. “I’m worried there is a tendency to see AI as a quick fix for students who are struggling in school,” he said.

“There’s no quick fix for learners who are from social deprived multiply disadvantaged backgrounds; I think we do need to invest in people and resources and time,” said Selwyn. “Tech can be part of that in the background, but I don’t think technology is ever going to be the solution to any kind of social disadvantage issue.”

It’s clear that AI is changing work, education and mindsets, but only careful consideration will ensure young people will have equal access to the careers they want.

As Luckin surmised: “Most of my time as an academic I believed AI would be a great tool for breaking down barriers, for greater inclusion, and it’s not rolling out that way at the moment, and we really need to be careful about that.”

title: Barnet council bringing Capita IT work in-house after alternative contract ‘abandoned’
raw_text:
Barnet Council will bring IT services in-house at the end of this month after being forced into an eleventh-hour decision to abandon its plan to switch supplier.

The London council U-turned on its plan to move IT to another company after the tender winner upped its costs and a subsequent review found that moving services in-house would have financial and service benefits.

In July 2022, the London borough announced it was ending its multi-layered outsourcing contract with business services giant Capita, originally signed in 2013. This followed members of the council’s policy and resources committee voting in favour of ending the contract.

The 10-year deal included human resources (HR), finance, IT and estates, as well as customer services and revenues and benefits. The arrangement was originally known as the One Barnet programme and was seen as a flagship for councils in the future.

But there were concerns over the quality of delivery of the contract over the years, with a 2018 report recommending that HR and finance services, then provided by Capita, should be brought back in-house.

Part of the plan to transition back to in-house services involved extending some contracts with Capita, including IT. The extended deal to deliver back-office services such as HR and finance, as well as deliver IT, was worth up to £57m.

The IT services element of the contract was set to move to another supplier on 1 October, but it will now move in-house by the end of this month (30 September) after that deal was cancelled.

Ultima Business Solutions was set to take over the contract, which was worth up to £10m, but the council decided to bring it in-house, stating that the bidder increased the cost.

Council meeting notes from earlier this month revealed that, “The council’s preferred bidder sought to substantially increase its submitted bid costs post submission and evaluation,” adding: “The preferred bidder was given the opportunity to either stand by its originally submitted bid or to withdraw its bid by a deadline set by the council. The bidder did not do this, and its bid was subsequently rejected by the council.”

As a result, Barnet carried out a due diligence service requirement review against the business case and delivery options, which identified the financial and service benefits of insourcing. “The procurement was subsequently abandoned,” said the council.

Barry Rawlings, leader of the council, said this week: “We are committed to providing the very best services for our residents that offer value for money and are accountable to Barnet Council taxpayers.

“By returning our IT service in-house, it allows the council to retain ownership of its technology operations, priorities and decision-making, as well as provide clearer accountability and greater control over security decisions, and improved alignment on cyber security.”

In 2022, Rawlings said IT, customer services, and revenues and benefits were more complicated to bring back in-house straight away, and contacts were extended.

Capita continued to deliver IT services until this month. “We thank our partners at Capita and welcome the transfer of staff to the council’s in-house team,” added Rawlings.

title: Digital Realty: Aaron Binkley’s passion and progress in sustainability
raw_text:
When Digital Realty’s vice-president of sustainability, Aaron Binkley, started out, sustainability and carbon emissions reduction wasn’t a big focus. Whether in the real-estate and architecture sector where he began, or in datacentres, the focus was typically more about maximising investments.

Today, he finds great satisfaction in leading Digital Realty’s sustainability collaborations and striving for higher standards globally, finding common ground in stakeholders’ differing perspectives to devise a true value proposition and communicate possible solutions.

“I practised architecture,” says Binkley, “I got licensed. I worked as an architect. And then after grad school, I stopped practising, and did sustainability programme work for a global company with a global portfolio.” 

Brought up on a small family farm in Pennsylvania next to an Amish community, he studied architecture at Carnegie Mellon University, and afterwards attended graduate school at its Centre for Building and Performance Diagnostics. 

While his family were neither eco-warrior nor Amish, he grew up understanding the need to steward the natural environment. However, 20 or so years ago, when Binkley started working in sustainability, environmentally focused collaborations and initiatives for better-designed buildings were scarcer than today. 

Clients often loved the idea of going green, but were less keen on the certification part. “I’d say, ‘well, you’re sort of missing the forest for the trees a little bit if you do that’,” he reveals. “That was one animating question for me, for grad school. Why aren’t more real-estate owners adopting this strategy that makes sense to me as an architect?”

There, Binkley researched, wrote and published a thesis on carbon – on how to monetise carbon credits for further investment in real-estate energy-efficiency projects. And that delivered Binkley’s first sustainability job. 

Kicking off a sustainability programme at globally focused warehousing company AMB Property, he built it up over several years, including through a merger. By then, times were changing – and something else was happening as well, namely big tech.

“I was in the Bay Area, headquartered in San Francisco, and I wasn’t doing anything technology-related,” says Binkley. “I was near Google and Meta, all these amazing companies, and it felt like a missed opportunity.”

Bridging the gap to tech

He surmised that datacentres might help him bridge the gap between tech and property, while remaining in sustainability. So, in 2014, he interviewed for the role of sustainability director at Digital Realty, which was seeking someone to take the helm of the global datacentre giant’s sustainability programme.

The operator already had “the bones of good practice”, says Binkley, having done some greener buildings and work on energy efficiency. And tech as a whole was increasingly feeling pressure to become greener and more energy efficient.

Indeed, Binkley cites Greenpeace’s Clicking Clean initiative in 2013 and 2014 as a driver.

“It was basically a muckraking initiative around ‘how green is the internet’ – your new iPhone, all the web searching that was all powered by coal and gas and polluting utility power sources – and asking what the likes of Microsoft, Amazon and Google were doing about that,” he says.

“And in their first report, they listed all the tech companies, including datacentre providers and Digital Realty. Most of them got a D or an F. It was a real warning for the tech industry.”

Binkley says Digital Realty vowed to do better. That meant they needed to figure out how to make improvements, which very quickly sent them out on the hunt for someone like him to ramp up sustainability company-wide.

“They saw that I understand industrial buildings, I understand office buildings, so I can understand the datacentre,” says Binkley. “It helped me get up to speed quickly, and it helps me have intelligent conversations with the teams in a real estate datacentre-focused company.”

The most rewarding part of the job? “I’m pretty proud of the renewable programme that Digital Realty’s built over the years. I think that’s been a very important part of our continued sustainability journey and success.”

The operator’s 2025 sustainability impact report reveals it achieved 93% renewable electricity, alongside an overall 1.38 PUE and 0.59 water usage effectiveness (WUE), while recycling 45% of its water. 

It also cut Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 68% from 2023, against a 42% reduction target. Its Scope 3 reduction target is 25% by 2030, although those emissions increased 28% in 2025; Digital Realty says that’s down to developing more datacentres.

It has assessed sustainability impacts across 59% of its suppliers and met sustainability certification standards for 1.5GW of its datacentre capacity. Revenue growth remains healthy. With more than 300 facilities across 30-odd countries, it reported an 18% quarterly jump in total revenues to $1.9bn (£1.4bn) in its Q2 2026, 29% up from the year-ago quarter.

Sustainability remains challenging

Achieving sustainability is challenging but enjoyable, Binkley concedes.

When he started, the operator did no renewables procurement. He steered them to start securing power purchase agreements with wind and solar farms. Key to that success, of course, was the ubiquitous theme of speaking the right language to the right stakeholders. Without that, it’s tough to garner executive support and involvement. Today, the programme has evolved across energy efficiency, water management and greener buildings.

When sustainability suddenly starts to make sense from the perspective of a whole team or even just an individual, the satisfaction can be enormous, says Binkley.

For example, in a previous role, he discovered lighting accounted for the lion’s share of energy consumption. The company didn’t understand this at first.

“The buildings mostly didn’t need air-conditioning,” says Binkley. “And while they had very small electrical loads, they had banks of lights in the ceiling, previously HID [high-intensity discharge] and metal halide.” 

Read more about Digital Realty

  • Digital Realty CTO on AI tokenomics and datacentre infrastructure: Chris Sharp talks up the pace of AI silicon innovation, the growth of inferencing workloads, and why boasting about datacentre megawatts misses the point.
  • Digital Realty doubles down on sustainability with pledge to cut carbon emissions by 2030: Colocation giant Digital Realty is embarking on a 10-year, business-wide carbon emissions reduction quest, led by climate science.

The solution was to replace them with more energy-efficient, controllable LEDs, which he saw as a no-brainer to do company-wide to save money and increase sustainability. 

They would say they understood, but kept raising objections – what about the costs, the schedules, the contractors? “There were all these ‘buts’, right? Like they weren’t convinced,” says Binkley. “And we were talking about lighting.”

Then, one manager in one market revealed that a long-term customer had moved out. They’d been in one building 20 years; it wasn’t in good condition. They’d lost their security deposit – and Digital Realty needed to renovate anyway before re-leasing.

It dawned that he could put the security deposit money into lighting. It would look nicer; a bright space instead of a dark cave. And he could tell the real-estate brokers the space was recently refurbished, including new high-efficiency lighting to keep costs low. It was like a switch went off in his head, says Binkley. “From that point on, every time we got space back from an old customer, it was standard practice,” he adds.

Other retrofits of energy-efficient lighting followed, cross-pollinating across Digital Realty’s various markets over time. Site staff became “less begrudging” of the change, and customers liked the better visibility as well.

“It was all in the service of how to empower people to figure out how something works for them, and finding ways to get the business excited about it,” he says. “That’s truly gratifying.”

Of course, there are less positive aspects too. Binkley is often dismayed by the extent of negative public discourse about datacentres, which has been “something of a gut punch”, he reveals.

“It is disheartening and even painful to experience when you and your peers are trying your hardest and to do the right thing around energy efficiency, emissions reduction and other environmental and sustainability issues,” says Binkley.

“We’re seeing a lot of this right now,” he says. “The story out there is not consistently accurate. I know that datacentres don’t all use that much water, for example.

“I’m a ‘by the facts’ kind of person by nature,” says Binkley. “I want to be well researched, accurate and technically correct, with the numbers at my fingertips, for good or for bad. But there are many misconceptions about datacentre impacts, what the industry is doing, and how much we care.”

Legacy of history

Some discourse may be the wages of history, says Binkley, of a general legacy of environmental destruction. Significant industrialisation over the past hundred years or so – from steel to automobiles, petrochemicals, aviation, to name a few sectors – rarely considered environmental impacts.

Expansion was prioritised. Major, heavy polluters didn’t clean up “after their messes”, leaving an environmental bill that in many cases has not even today been calculated, let alone paid for or redressed. “We now need to clean up all these sites that were contaminated, and decarbonise these industries after the fact,” he says.

All that said, from the early days, the datacentre industry was one that was sourcing renewable energy and trying to be efficient. Binkley notes that even from 2013 or 2014, many datacentre companies were committing to cleaner energy and decarbonisation. This often went beyond what other sectors were doing.

“What other industry has grown from its earliest stages with clear, definable, accountable environmental commitments?” he asks. “I don’t think that even 20 years ago another high-growth industry would have built that in. So, it feels like a gut punch when people say you’re the worst industry out there now, when we’ve been a major buyer of clean energy in the world for many years.”

title: Will new grid rules put the future of UK datacentres at risk?
raw_text:
Planning, land availability and construction costs remain significant considerations for datacentre developers. Increasingly, however, the critical issue is power. 

With 315 datacentres reported as currently waiting for grid connections and overall demand for electricity continuing to rise, securing energy capacity has become one of the most important factors determining whether a project proceeds at all. To put it simply, the amount and size of datacentres vying for connection to the UK’s electrical grid is too high.

To address this problem for datacentres, the options are to increase the availability and supply of power and the infrastructure required to deliver it, or reduce the number and scale of datacentres requiring power. The availability of power and the infrastructure required to deliver it is increasing as part of the Great Grid Upgrade, meaning the supply side of the equation is being addressed. But this is a long-term solution and won’t fix the immediate pressures of this supply and demand equation.

Developer commitment fees

Ofgem has opted to try to reduce demand for electrical connections by proposing the introduction of datacentre commitment fees, that require large datacentre developments to commit significant capital when accepting a grid connection offer. The regulator hopes the requirement for such fees will help remove speculative projects that are occupying scarce network capacity, and the fee is expected to apply retrospectively to projects that already hold a grid connection. The public consultation on the proposed introduction of commitment fees is scheduled to close on 16 September. That raises an important question: will it distinguish effectively between projects which are viable and can stomach an upfront fee, and those which are not and cannot?

The backdrop to the Ofgem consultation is a grid connection system under substantial strain,  with the government's AI and digital infrastructure ambitions driving further demand for increasingly power-intensive facilities. For example, Ofgem has said datacentres account for around 73GW of power within the connection queue, which exceeds the UK's peak national electricity demand by a considerable margin. This drive for delivery without the necessary infrastructure in place puts the sector in a difficult position.

The logic behind the proposed commitment fees is therefore understandable. Developers would be required to make an upfront payment equivalent to between 2.5% and 7.5% of average project costs when accepting a connection offer, with the fee returned when the facility is operational but forfeited if the project leaves the queue before completion. In principle, this should discourage developers from securing connection offers without a realistic prospect of progressing the scheme.

Nevertheless, the proposal risks oversimplifying the realities of datacentre development. Most projects do not simply move from grid offer to construction. Developers typically spend considerable time resolving planning issues, undertaking technical surveys, negotiating land rights, engaging with prospective operators and securing investment before significant capital is committed. Requiring substantial sums to be paid at an earlier stage may remove speculative projects, but it may also prevent viable schemes from advancing.

Additionally, if developers are required to commit substantial capital years before projects become operational, some may begin to assess opportunities elsewhere. Grid constraints are a challenge across Europe, but investors ultimately compare locations on the basis of cost, certainty and speed of delivery. While these proposals alone are unlikely to drive developers overseas, they could influence those already deliberating a move, deterring investment and contradicting the government’s pledge to make the UK an AI leader.

Behind the meter strategies

Another consequence may be a growing shift towards alternative power strategies. Interest in behind-the-meter or private wire arrangements has increased significantly as developers seek greater certainty over power availability. 

Rather than relying exclusively on a conventional grid connection, operators are increasingly exploring opportunities to source electricity directly from private generation assets, including solar farms and dedicated gas-fired generation, supported by large-scale on-site storage. Initially, these arrangements were viewed as a temporary means of overcoming connection delays but increasingly they are becoming a central part of development strategy.

Behind-the-meter solutions, however, come with their own complexities and are not a straightforward substitute for a grid connection. Datacentres require continuous and highly reliable power supplies that renewable energy alone cannot always provide, particularly with the levels of resilience required by facilities operating around the clock. As a result, many developers are exploring hybrid solutions that combine private generation assets with conventional, reduced, grid connections, battery storage and backup generation – not to avoid the grid altogether but to reduce dependence upon it.

From a legal perspective, this introduces additional complexity in securing power supply agreements or further land rights for connection infrastructure, and makes it important for developers to ensure regulatory compliance in the supply of electricity and avoid long-term operational risk – all of which become increasingly important components of project development.

Don't wait and see

The consultation on the introduction of datacentre commitment fees does address other alternatives, including the phased return of commitment fee capital as schemes reach defined milestones, allowing developers to demonstrate progress before recovering portions of their investment. Another possible option is milestone-based payment requirements, where additional financial commitments are triggered as a project advances, rather than requiring a substantial upfront payment. These approaches could provide a more proportionate means of distinguishing between non-viable schemes and genuine developments that require time to secure planning permission, financing, customers and land rights.

Whilst the consultation remains ongoing, adopting a wait-and-see approach is not an attractive option. Existing projects should be reviewed to understand the potential impact of commitment fees and to assess whether alternative energy strategies could support future developments. It’s also important for developers to consider contributing to the consultation process itself. There may be scope for a more balanced approach that the industry could advocate for, such as phased returns of capital or milestone-based requirements, which distinguish between speculative and genuine projects without creating unnecessary barriers to investment.

The challenge is to ensure that measures designed to remove non-viable projects do not discourage the investment needed to support the UK's digital economy. As demand for AI infrastructure continues to grow, access to power is rapidly becoming as important as access to capital. How the regulator chooses to balance those competing pressures may have a significant influence on the future direction of the UK's datacentre market.

Peter Dilks is energy and real estate partner at law firm Shakespeare Martineau.

title: Selective sovereignty: Why balance beats lockdown in the data debate
raw_text:
Ask how far an enterprise should go to keep its data sovereign, and it often resolves to picking a side – hold everything inside a trusted region, or keep drawing on the speed and scale of the global cloud.

Patrick Smith, chief technology officer of Everpure, argues the more useful answer lies somewhere in-between.

Smith is the latest senior storage figure to answer questions on data sovereignty. He works through the same questions posed to the earlier contributors in this series, individually and at length.

In this article we set out his answers, which cohere around a single argument for selective sovereignty: precise, workload-by-workload choices that apply strong controls where risk runs highest, while continuing to use global platforms where they add the most.

It is a case for balance rather than lockdown – and it adds another voice to the debate running through this series on data sovereignty.

TL;DR – Everpure’s Patrick Smith on data sovereignty

  • Sovereignty is not just borders, cyber security or compliance – it is lifecycle control.
  • Location still matters, but it no longer settles anything.
  • Closed data blocs are not inevitable; regional influence is.
  • Residency does not equal sovereignty – but neither does all-or-nothing lockdown.
  • AI outputs inherit sovereignty; prompts and context can leak it.
  • Precise choices, not maximum restriction, create the advantage.

The assumption trap

Smith begins where the series began, with the assumptions enterprises still carry. “The most outdated assumptions are that data sovereignty is primarily a question of keeping information inside a national border, satisfying a cyber security requirement or ensuring compliance with regulation,” he says. “That view is too narrow for today’s world.”

Across the next 12 to 18 months, he argues, the real test is whether an organisation holds visibility, governance and control over the whole data lifecycle. That means, “understanding where data is stored and processed, who can access it, which jurisdictions and regulations apply, and whether the organisation can continue operating if a provider or service becomes unavailable”.

Location, in other words, still matters, but it doesn’t settle everything. “An organisation can store data locally and still have limited or ineffective sovereignty if it does not understand who operates the platform, who controls access, which legal jurisdictions apply, or how data can be managed and recovered,” says Smith.

A question of balance

On whether the world is fragmenting into distinct data blocs, Smith is measured. “We may see more regional influence over how sensitive data is stored, processed and transferred, but that does not necessarily mean a world of closed data blocs,” he says.

Cross-border flows and global cloud, hyperscaler and software as a service (SaaS) offerings, he argues, will remain crucial where they meet business and regulatory requirements.

That leads to the line that defines his argument. “Data residency does not equal data sovereignty, and at the same time an all-or-nothing approach to sovereignty would mean losing access to valuable global platforms,” he says. “A balance is definitely required.”

The AI inheritance

The balance test sharpens when artificial intelligence (AI) enters the frame. Smith’s answer to whether sovereignty extends to models, outputs and derived data is blunt: “It’s safest to assume that sovereignty considerations extend beyond the original dataset.”

The outputs of AI models may contain sensitive information or reveal strategic intent.

The practical risk, he argues, sits in inference rather than training. “Organisations need to understand whether models are deployed locally or accessed as global services, and whether sensitive prompts and context are leaving the sovereign environment.”

For organisations that lean on retrieval-augmented generation, that means validating what an inference workload can actually reach.

Policy, not parallel stacks

Smith’s architectural answer to operating across jurisdictions is a unified one. He points to Everpure’s Enterprise Data Cloud vision – which brings data together across on-premise, public cloud and hybrid environments “through a unified data plane and managed by an intelligent control plane” – combined with governance software that can “discover, classify and contextualise data wherever it resides”.

The aim is to govern by policy rather than build a separate stack for every regime. “This approach can help with sovereignty as it enables the use of policy to govern data placement, access, protection, replication and recovery across locations and workloads, rather than creating a separate technology stack for every jurisdiction,” he explains.

The result, says Smith, is “a cloud-like operating model” that applies stronger controls to the most sensitive workloads while still drawing on public cloud where it adds most.

Control, in this reading, means visibility and authority: the power to “decide where data is held, who can access it, how it is used, where it can move, how it is protected, and how it can be recovered or removed”.

Most models fall short, he says, when organisations cannot see “the location of all data and potential copies, the jurisdiction of the operator, privileged access, metadata handling, portability or recovery options”.

The value of precision

The commercial pay-off, argues Smith, does not come from maximum restriction. “Competitive advantage won’t come from adopting the most restrictive environment,” he says. “It will come from making precise choices – keeping critical and sensitive assets within appropriate levels of control whilst leveraging global providers where they can add speed, scale, functionality and innovation.”

Done well, says Smith, a sovereignty strategy supports customer trust, participation in regulated markets, protection of proprietary information and confidence in AI adoption.

Looking ahead, he expects a selective rather than a maximalist end state. “We’ll start to see sensitive and high-risk data staying in-region by default, and AI systems will need to be transparent about data origin and handling requirements,” says Smith.

The sovereignty service-level agreement, by contrast, “could emerge more gradually over time as the industry fine-tunes procurement and contractual commitments covering location, access, operator accountability, portability, incident response and recovery”.

For Smith, the trajectory is clear. Sovereignty is not a wall; it is a dial – and the enterprises that win will be the ones that learn to turn it precisely.

Ask how far an enterprise should go to keep its data sovereign, and it often resolves to picking a side – hold everything inside a trusted region, or keep drawing on the speed and scale of the global cloud.

Patrick Smith, chief technology officer of Everpure, argues the more useful answer lies somewhere in-between.

Smith is the latest senior storage figure to answer questions on data sovereignty. He works through the same questions posed to the earlier contributors in this series, individually and at length.

In this article we set out his answers, which cohere around a single argument for selective sovereignty: precise, workload-by-workload choices that apply strong controls where risk runs highest, while continuing to use global platforms where they add the most.

It is a case for balance rather than lockdown – and it adds another voice to the debate running through this series on data sovereignty.

TL;DR – Everpure’s Patrick Smith on data sovereignty

  • Sovereignty is not just borders, cyber security or compliance – it is lifecycle control.
  • Location still matters, but it no longer settles anything.
  • Closed data blocs are not inevitable; regional influence is.
  • Residency does not equal sovereignty – but neither does all-or-nothing lockdown.
  • AI outputs inherit sovereignty; prompts and context can leak it.
  • Precise choices, not maximum restriction, create the advantage.

The assumption trap

Smith begins where the series began, with the assumptions enterprises still carry. “The most outdated assumptions are that data sovereignty is primarily a question of keeping information inside a national border, satisfying a cyber security requirement or ensuring compliance with regulation,” he says. “That view is too narrow for today’s world.”

Across the next 12 to 18 months, he argues, the real test is whether an organisation holds visibility, governance and control over the whole data lifecycle.

On 22 September 2026, Computer Weekly turns 60. To mark the milestone, we asked some of our friends - experts, parliamentarians, IT leaders and suppliers - for their perspectives on how tech has changed their lives over six decades. What's changed the most for you since then?

I didn’t study computer science, nor am I a tech bro or even technically minded for that matter, and yet somehow “tech” became my entire working life.

For a period, it even brought me into the Computer Weekly family as marketing director for a little over a year. Computer Weekly reaching its 60th anniversary is testament to its adaptability: from a printed, weekly magazine to now a key cog in a larger, digital machine - throughout which its influence has barely waned.

That evolution is something I relate to, closely mirroring my own in the media industry we share, one which has been disrupted possibly more than any other.

Australian beginnings

I grew up in Australia, and despite the university HTML classes I never attended and our introduction to the network protocol tool called Gopher, tech was far from my mind. Unsure what to do after my studies, I worked as a civil servant for a few years, and we had our own, proprietary (and rudimentary) version of email. But no internet, yet.

The event that would change this course landed serendipitously. I found a junior position selling advertising for the broadsheet newspaper, the Sydney Morning Herald, a venerated, 195-year-old institution. It was 2004 and salespeople were selling print classifieds to car yards and real estate agents, while a separate team would offer those same businesses a wonderful new “digital ad” as an add-on for free. In hindsight, it seems nuts. Although I recall we were puzzled in 2005 when the publisher of our magazine division left to join Google, curious why you’d ever leave such a prestigious institution.

Before long I was in tech media with Haymarket, a magazine publisher owned and operated by Michael Heseltine. In Australia, we published the gadget mag PC Authority, gamer and overclocking fanboy ‘zine Atomic MPC (Maximum Power Computing!), the industry rag Computer Reseller News and business coverage via IT News.

For the next six years, tech was everything I needed to know.

It was an intense period of speculation and discovery. Our British overlords sent a younger crew from headquarters to watch over the rowdy Australians. Many were just out of college and shared their lives with friends “back home” via Facebook following its launch there in late 2006.

We heard about the viral Twitter breakout at SXSW in March 2007 and I became an early user for both work and play, convincing many journalist colleagues to do the same.

The first iPod touch - the precursor of the iPhone - came into the office for editorial review in September 2007 and we all crowded around in utter amazement, taking turns to swipe here and there.

Nintendo sent some Wii games for review in late 2007, but no console. I called their PR and suggested that if they didn’t ship us one by the end of the week, Atomic MPC would review the box the game came in and its requisite cartridge.

I wrongly predicted that Microsoft’s Zune would take over from the iPod as it was a superior product - I maintain this latter point of view.

I didn’t buy a phone for many years. I’d just drop in on the gadget review team and walk away with something to replace the last one.

Media is a tough old business, and while Australia is a vast country it is also isolated. Tech media gave me the chance to see the rest of the world.

To London's Tech City

I moved to the UK in 2012 and while living with a startup founder in East London became immersed in the local startup community. It was the period of Silicon Roundabout, London’s Tech City, and Silicon Drinkabout. I looked out for cool startups to help on my weekends and spoke with many “blockchain for laundry” wantrepreneurs.

But I was also one of the early beta testers of Revolut. Having found them through Seedcamp, I even pitched them to help with marketing and met the only three members of the team in Level 39 in Canary Wharf.

I arrived at TechTarget as marketing director for Computer Weekly, among others, in February, 2015.

We took the new Women in Tech event from a few dozen people to a couple of hundred by aligning with London Tech Week and had it trending on Twitter - when that was still a big thing. A year later, we were planning Computer Weekly’s 50th anniversary celebrations. How time flies, eh? The poor editor Bryan Glick even had to traipse around London with me, looking for venues. 

French unicorns to US Midwest

I soon moved to France and jumped on its startup train, founding a marketing company called Iytro that provided part-time CMOs for early stage startups. We worked with some of the biggest and brightest in their field, many of whom have gone on to build unicorns and I sold it in 2023.

Now I find myself in the US, at a pivotal point in the story of what role tech plays in our lives. I am building my own tech media business called StartMidwest.

The heartland of the country has vast plains and huge, global historical companies, but tech growth on the coasts has seemingly passed it by. As re-industrialisation becomes a buzzword, robotics and AI are becoming deeply embedded in manufacturing and other essential industries. A nascent startup scene full of entrepreneurship and innovation aims to ensure the region fulfils its potential and keeps its best talent. We’re here to document it.

I’ve made my life working around tech - from machines and gadgets to the entrepreneurs changing our world, and I’ve done most of it from within the media industry. Tech has disrupted the world, and media has been one of the most disrupted of all industries.

I’m just glad to have had a front-row seat.

title: CW@60: Geek is good (eventually) – a social journey through technology
raw_text:
On 22 September 2026, Computer Weekly turns 60. To mark the milestone, we asked some of our friends - experts, parliamentarians, IT leaders and suppliers - for their perspectives on how tech has changed their lives over six decades. What's changed the most for you since then?

There is not enough space in a weighty book, let alone in one article, to detail all the incredible milestones that technology has achieved during the 60 years that Computer Weekly has been covering the sector.

There’s even more to come, of course. Even those 60 years will one day be looked back on as a time of mere baby steps in the digital revolution that continues to transform the way we live and work.

Artificial intelligence is the next accelerant. Quantum computing won’t be far behind. The advances in science and bioengineering and genetics and healthcare and robotics that will come in future will make the iPhone seem quaint.

I could pick many or any of the key tech developments of the past six decades as the one that impacted my digital lifetime and tell you a story about why. But that’s not the thing that, on reflection, stands out for me.

Not cool

One of the memorable moments of my first trip to India as a technology journalist in the early 2000s was sitting in a bar in Bangalore / Bengaluru with a couple of 20-something Indian lads – graduates from one of India’s excellent technology colleges - and listening to them tell me how working in IT helped them to meet girls. For young Indians, IT was cool.

This had not been my experience.

Like many in this trade, I was an accidental technology journalist. Many of us joke that nobody grew up wanting to be a “tech journo”. In fact, I was an accidental technologist even before that.

I ended up doing a computer science degree, simply because I thought it would be less boring than the maths degree I had originally signed up to. Sitting in a lecture theatre one day in my late teens, listening to a professor explaining the proof of why one is greater than zero, I realised there were some things in the world I was happy to accept as truth. One being greater than zero was one such fact.

Thanks to a common first year for the two courses, I switched to computer science, little realising I had set my path in reinforced concrete.

As a university student, my most common experience of studying tech came frequently. I’d be in a bar or at a party, chatting with people, making new friends, maybe even meeting a pleasant young lady. The conversation was going well. Laughter. Maybe a bit of flirtation. But all along I knew – eventually, the question would come.

“So, what do you study?”

“I’m doing computer science.”

“Oh…”

There endeth the conversation. Honestly – I can’t tell you how often that exact scenario played out. Computers were not cool.

Growth mode

In the late 1980s when I was job hunting, the UK IT sector was in growth mode. There were jobs aplenty – it was the obvious way to go for a computer science graduate. But I knew tech was not my long-term future, so I rejected the offers of programming roles and joined a trainee scheme that would lead to a job in sales. Learn to sell computers and I could sell anything, or so I hoped.

“In the 60 years of Computer Weekly, tech has gone from a dark and dull art, conducted in dingy basements, usually by middle-aged men with beards, to the most transformational and talked-about force on the planet”

Bryan Glick

Outside of work, the nineties were my dinner party years. Round a friend’s house, meeting new people, chatting before the food was served. Eventually, the question would come.

“So, what do you do?”

“I work in IT.”

“Oh…”

You never forget the look on someone’s face, when they realise their place at the dinner table for the next couple of hours was next to the geek who worked in IT.

Get those transferable skills in sales, go get a job in another sector that wasn’t as uncool as IT. That was the plan.

Gamekeeper turns poacher

Ten years later, after an only occasionally successful stint in selling IT, it turned out to be the sales skills I left behind as I switched careers and became a tech journalist. Gamekeeper turned poacher, writing about the flaws, frailties and failures of the industry in which I had previously worked.

Journalism is a sociable job – you meet lots of new people. And things took a turn for the better.

“So, what do you do?”

“I’m a journalist.”

“Really? That’s so interesting. What do you write about?”

“I write about technology.”

“Oh…”

Those extra few seconds of conversation before reaching the inevitable geek-alert moment were precious.

Of course, during much of the noughties, my goal was to develop my journalistic skills and move to a publication that didn’t write about tech. And of course, that didn’t happen. One look at my CV and all any recruiter saw was COMPUTERS.

Something big

Move forward another 10 years, by which time I was incredibly fortunate to be the editor in chief of Computer Weekly, with all the responsibility and career satisfaction that came from running the best-known brand in business technology publishing. And yes, things had changed.

“So, what do you do?”

“I’m a journalist.”

“Really? That’s so interesting. What do you write about?”

“I write about technology.”

“Ooh – which iPhone do you think I should buy?”

Well, it was an improvement. I at least got to reply, “I have no idea,” before the conversation began its downward drift. But it was the start of something big.

Another 10 years pass. It’s the 2020s. My joints ache more in the mornings, but I can enter the social side of the profession and even outside of work with a spring in my step. Why?

“So, what do you do?”

“I’m a journalist.”

“Really? That’s so interesting. What do you write about?”

“I write about technology.”

“Oh, wow – you must have so much to write about, there’s so much going in the tech world, isn’t there?”

And yes, dear reader - on occasions it has happened. My conversational partner would pause, and in that brief moment of silence unwittingly reveal the gravity – to me, at least - of what they were about to say.

“…That’s so cool.”

I knew it

Ladies and gentlemen – tech is cool. I *coughs* always knew it. And I’m so glad I stuck with it – and that it stuck with me.

In the 60 years of Computer Weekly – in my 60 years – tech has gone from a dark and dull art, conducted in dingy basements, usually by middle-aged men with beards, to the most transformational and talked-about force on the planet.

It was always that, of course – but perceptions matter. The perception of tech has changed, and in doing so it changed my life.

Geek is good.

title: CW@60: AI will change the economics of business more profoundly than the cloud
raw_text:
On 22 September 2026, Computer Weekly turns 60. To mark the milestone, we asked some of our friends - experts, parliamentarians, IT leaders and suppliers - for their perspectives on how tech has changed their lives over six decades. What's changed the most for you since then?

I have spent most of my working life watching technology change what it means to run a business.

When I started my career at Oracle in 1987, one of the assumptions that shaped business strategy was: the larger the company, the greater the advantage. This was especially true when it came to enterprise-grade software. It had to be installed, maintained, patched, upgraded, and integrated, which meant that it required resources that were often out of reach of smaller, growing businesses.

The cloud began to change that relationship by shifting much of the burden of running technology from the customer to the provider. As a result, a growing company could manage financials, inventory, customers, commerce, and reporting on the same kind of systems that had previously demanded much larger resources. Or put another way, a smaller company could operate with the sophistication, intelligence, and capacity once reserved for the world's largest enterprises without first becoming one.

This was a huge part of the opportunity we saw when we started NetSuite in 1998 - businesses should be able to use sophisticated software without having to own and operate all the infrastructure underneath it. As I look ahead, I believe what’s happening with artificial intelligence (AI) could have an even bigger impact on the economics of competition.

From the economics of technology to the economics of work

For decades, when a company expanded it became more complex, and the answer was usually to add capacity. More transactions meant more people. More markets meant more managers, systems, and coordination. More data meant larger analytics teams. Growth and organisational complexity tended to rise together. AI changes that equation.

In finance, for example, AI can help teams understand what is changing in the business before the month-end close. It can surface anomalies, identify patterns, and support forecasting without requiring the same level of manual analysis. A change in margin, cash flow, or revenue is rarely just a finance event. It can reflect changes in customer demand, pricing, inventory availability, production costs, or fulfillment performance. Connecting finance to the underlying operational reality is therefore critical to AI performance.

“The next generation of companies may have the reach, intelligence, control, and operating capacity of far larger organisations, while retaining the speed and agility of businesses a fraction of their size”

Evan Goldberg

AI can help companies interpret customer activity, manage inventory, forecast demand, and coordinate workflows. When these activities are connected in the same business system, AI can reason across them - linking a financial result to the orders, customers, supply, inventory, and operational decisions that produced it. That means companies can add new capabilities, enter new markets, or introduce new business models without growing their operations and costs at the same rate.

That changes the maths of growth. This is why I think AI will ultimately have a greater impact on the economics of running a business than the cloud. The cloud made enterprise technology more accessible. AI has the potential to do the same for enterprise capability.

The result may be a new kind of organisation - a company with the operational capabilities of a much larger business, but with the speed and agility of a smaller one.

AI still needs context

Stepping back, while AI changes many things, it does not eliminate the need for good business systems. In fact, it makes them more important.

The best AI still depends on the quality of the data and context it can access. It depends on having a connected, historical understanding of how a particular business operates. If data is incomplete, inconsistent, or disconnected, AI can only perform as well as the information available to it. A connected business suite gives AI a shared context across financials, customers, inventory, people, and workflows, allowing it to reason across the business rather than in isolated silos.

If AI is going to help operate a company, it needs reliable information about customers, orders, inventory, employees, revenue, and cash. It needs to understand how those records relate over time: which customers buy which products, what demand does to supply, how orders flow into revenue, and where operational decisions affect financial outcomes. It also needs to understand permissions, controls, and which actions people and technology are authorised to take. A trusted system of record becomes the foundation from which AI can reason, plan, and execute.

A different shape of company

Every major computing shift changes more than the technology itself. The PC changed who could access computing power. The internet changed how information moved. The cloud changed where computing happened and who could afford sophisticated business applications. Mobile changed how computing fit into daily life.

They also all have one other thing in common. Each of these eras began with the promise to level the playing field for smaller, growing organisations by democratising access to technology, but in the end the winners were “large” enterprises.

In contrast, the winners created by AI might not follow the traditional enterprise definition - thousands of employees, multiple layers of management, specialised departments, large budgets, complex systems - and instead just operate like them.

The next generation of companies may have the reach, intelligence, control, and operating capacity of far larger organisations, while retaining the speed and agility of businesses a fraction of their size.

The cloud allowed companies to use enterprise technology without first becoming enterprises. When grounded in a connected record of the whole business, AI can allow them to acquire enterprise capability without taking on enterprise complexity. Having watched the cloud reshape the technology industry, AI could reshape the economics of business itself.

Evan Goldberg is founder and executive vice president at Oracle NetSuite.

Más allá del enfoque de "implementar y olvidar" del proveedor, la solución proporciona a los equipos de TI empresariales una plataforma escalable orientada al ciclo de vida para manejar los cambios de infraestructura y la remediación relacionada en entornos de TI híbridos.

raw_text: ลอนดอน, Sept. 22, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- SASE OpsLab Ltd มาร์เก็ตเพลสระบบอัตโนมัติ SASE ที่ขับเคลื่อนด้วยซอฟต์แวร์ ประกาศเปิดตัวแพลตฟอร์มเวอร์ชันล่าสุดในวันนี้ ซึ่งออกแบบมาเพื่อรับมือกับการบริหารจัดการวงจรชีวิตโครงสร้างพื้นฐาน SASE ในระยะยาว โซลูชันนี้ก้าวข้ามแนวทาง "ปรับใช้แล้วปล่อยทิ้ง" ของผู้จำหน่าย โดยมอบแพลตฟอร์มที่รองรับการปรับขนาดและมุ่งเน้นการบริหารจัดการตลอดวงจรชีวิตให้แก่ทีมไอที ระดับองค์กร เพื่อจัดการการเปลี่ยนแปลงของโครงสร้างพื้นฐานและการแก้ไขปัญหาที่เกี่ยวข้องในสภาพแวดล้อม Hybrid IT

title: SASE OpsLab Ltd Launches industry first Lifecycle Management Platform simplifying Hybrid SASE Build&Run Operations
raw_text: LONDON, Sept. 22, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- SASE OpsLab Ltd , the software-driven SASE automation marketplace, today announced its latest platform release, designed to tackle long-term SASE infrastructure lifecycle management.
